Jake Calloway rides into Red Mesa with a branding iron and trouble with the railroad boss.

But a branding iron changed everything. When Jake Calloway showed it — a branding iron, genuine, legal, undeniable — the room went quiet. It was proof. Proof that the railroad boss's claim was a lie, and lies, in Red Mesa, have a short life.

That night in the saloon, the railroad boss's men made their play: cards, insults, a gun cleared half out of leather. Jake Calloway ended it without firing — the fast peace, the telegraph operator called it later, shaking their head.

the telegraph operator dug up the records: the original survey, the territorial seal, the witness — old, afraid, but honest. a branding iron matched, link by link. the railroad boss's forgery claim started to look like what it was: desperation.

the railroad boss came at noon, as villains do, with lawyers and gunmen in equal number. 'a branding iron is a forgery,' the railroad boss declared. 'And forgers hang.' The town watched from windows. Red Mesa held its breath again.

Thursday night they came with fire. The livery burned, and a branding iron's copies with it — but Jake Calloway had the original where fire couldn't reach. the railroad boss had played the last card. Friday would tell.

CHAPTER 3: High Noon

the railroad boss stepped out with two gunmen. 'Last chance,' the railroad boss said. 'Ride out.' Jake Calloway thought of Red Mesa, of the telegraph operator, of every small place that ever needed one person to stand. 'No,' Jake Calloway said.

What happened next took four seconds and would be told for forty years. When the dust settled, the railroad boss's gunmen were down — winged, not killed; Jake Calloway never shot to kill if winging would do — and the railroad boss stood alone, empty-handed.

The hearing went ahead anyway, because Jake Calloway insisted on it. Law, not guns. a branding iron was examined, the witness testified, the seal was verified. The judge — even the railroad boss's judge — couldn't lie with the whole town watching.

CHAPTER 4: The Drive

They reached the railhead with the herds and the deed and their heads high. Red Mesa was solvent. Red Mesa was free. Jake Calloway looked back at the dust of the trail and felt the peculiar ache of a job done.

the railroad boss's rustlers hit them at the canyon — the last play of a losing hand. The fight was short and decisive: the town rode together, and together is a word the railroad boss never understood.

the railroad boss wasn't done — the breed never is. The cattle were driven off in the night, the water rights challenged, the railroad brought in. Red Mesa needed more than a verdict; it needed a future.

Red Mesa threw a dance. the telegraph operator danced every dance. The schoolteacher cried. The blacksmith forged a branding iron's likeness in iron for the courthouse wall — 'so nobody forgets,' he said.
